etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English spot, spotte, partially from Middle Dutch spotte (“spot, speck”), and partially merging with Middle English splot, from Old English splott (“spot, plot of land”), from Proto-West Germanic *splott, from Proto-Germanic *spluttaz (“segment”), from Proto-Indo-European *splt-no- (“an off-split, segment”), from Proto-Indo-European *(s)pel- (“to split”). Cognate with North Frisian spot (“speck, piece of ground”), Low German spot (“speck”), Old Norse spotti (“small piece”). See also splot, splotch.

definitions.definition: A round or irregular patch on the surface of a thing having a different color, texture etc. and generally round in shape.
A stain or disfiguring mark.
A pimple, papule or pustule.
A symbol on a playing card, domino, die, etc. indicating its value; a pip.
A small, unspecified amount or quantity.
(slang, US) A bill of five-dollar or ten-dollar denomination in dollars.
A location or area.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book III”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: That spot to which I point is Paradise.
"A jolly place," said he, "in times of old! / But something ails it now: the spot is curs'd."

quote.citation: 2011, Tom Fordyce, Rugby World Cup 2011: England 12-19 France‎[1]:
quote.text: Yachvilli made it 6-0 with a second sweet strike from 45 metres after Matt Stevens was penalised for collapsing a scrum, and then slid another penalty just wide from the same spot.

definitions.definition: A parking space.

quote.citation: 2011 March 23, “We asked mayoral candidates: Do you support 'dibs' on parking spots?”, in Chicago Sun-Times:
quote.text: Del Valle has the blessing of a garage, so he doesn't have to claim “dibs” on shoveled street spots himself, he said.

definitions.definition: (sports) An official determination of placement.
A bright lamp; a spotlight.
(US, advertising) A brief advertisement or program segment on television.
A difficult situation.
(gymnastics, dance, weightlifting) One who spots (supports or assists a maneuver, or is prepared to assist if safety dictates); a spotter.
(soccer) Penalty spot.

quote.citation: 2011 January 8, Chris Bevan, “Arsenal 1 - 1 Leeds”, in BBC‎[2]:
quote.text: The Gunners dominated for long periods but, against the run of play, Denilson fouled Max Gradel and Robert Snodgrass put Leeds ahead from the spot.

definitions.definition: The act of spotting or noticing something.
A variety of the common domestic pigeon, so called from a spot on its head just above the beak.
A food fish (Leiostomus xanthurus) of the Atlantic coast of the United States, with a black spot behind the shoulders and fifteen oblique dark bars on the sides.
The southern redfish, or red horse (Sciaenops ocellatus), which has a spot on each side at the base of the tail.
(in the plural, brokers' slang, dated) Commodities, such as merchandise and cotton, sold for immediate delivery.
(physics) An autosoliton.
(finance) A decimal point; point.
Any of various points marked on the table, from which balls are played, in snooker, pool, billiards, etc.
Any of the balls marked with spots in the game of pool, which one player aims to pot, the other player taking the stripes.
(transitive) To see, find; to pick out, notice, locate, distinguish or identify.

quote.citation: 2020 July 1, Ruth Sutherland, Neil Peters, “Answering the call”, in Rail, page 47:
quote.text: The campaign aimed to give commuters the confidence to trust their own instincts and intervene if they spot someone vulnerable who may be at risk of suicide, and to talk to them to interrupt their suicidal thoughts.

definitions.definition: (US, slang, ditransitive) To loan a small amount of money to someone.

quote.citation: 2018, Tayari Jones, An American Marriage, Oneworld Publications, page 185:
quote.text: “It’s close to payday, but you’re welcome to what I have. Maybe Wickliffe can spot me a few.”

definitions.definition: (transitive, intransitive) To stain; to leave a spot (on).
(transitive) To cover with spots, to speckle.

quote.citation: 1865, Walt Whitman, “When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d”, in Sequel to Drum-Taps: When Lilacs Last in the Dooryard Bloom’d and other poems:
quote.text: […]  Amid lanes and through old woods, where lately the violets peep’d from the ground, spotting the gray debris,  […]

definitions.definition: (transitive) To remove, or attempt to remove, a stain.
(transitive) To retouch a photograph on film to remove minor flaws.
(transitive, gymnastics, dance, weightlifting, climbing) To support or assist a maneuver, or to be prepared to assist if safety dictates.

quote.citation: 1989 April 15, Angela Bowen, “Towards a National Lesbian Conference”, in Gay Community News, page 2:
quote.text: There had not been time to build handrails, so lines of women spotted the sides of the ramp.

definitions.definition: (transitive, dance) To keep the head and eyes pointing in a single direction while turning.
(transitive) To stain; to blemish; to taint; to disgrace; to tarnish, as reputation.

quote.citation: a. 1587, Philippe Sidnei [i.e., Philip Sidney], “(please specify the folio)”, in [Fulke Greville; Matthew Gwinne; John Florio], editors, The Countesse of Pembrokes Arcadia [The New Arcadia], London:  […]  [John Windet] for William Ponsonbie, published 1590, →OCLC:
quote.text: Link not me in self same chain / With the wicked-working folk, / Who their spotted thoughts do cloak.

quote.citation: c. 1608–1610, Francis Beaumont, John Fletcher, “Philaster: Or, Love Lies a Bleeding”, in Comedies and Tragedies […], London:  […]  Humphrey Robinson, […], and for Humphrey Moseley […], published 1679, →OCLC, Act V, scene ii:
quote.text: If ever I shall close these eyes but once, / May I live spotted for my perjury.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To cut or chip (timber) in preparation for hewing.
(transitive, chiefly snooker and billiards) To place (an object) at a location indicated by a spot.
(intransitive, snooker and billiards) Of a ball, to be capable of being placed on its own spot.
(aviation, military, transitive) To position (an aircraft) on the deck of an aircraft carrier ready for launch by catapult.

quote.citation: 1959, Aviation Boatswain's Mate 3 & 2: Navy Training Courses, United States. Bureau of Naval Personnel, page 315:
quote.text: The aircraft is spotted on the catapult, and the console operator turns the crank to FIRST READY, causing the exhaust valve to close.

This spotting order varies from carrier to carrier to suit the flight-deck layout. Certain aircraft must be spotted in a specific location to permit servicing, loading of ammunition, starting, maintenance, and so forth.

definitions.definition: (rail transport, transitive) To position (a locomotive or car) at a predetermined point, e.g., for loading or unloading.
(commerce, finance) Available on the spot; for immediate payment or delivery.
